claim: Schizophrenia affects around 1% of the global population.
source: Schizophrenia is a complex and chronic psychiatric disorder affecting around 1% of the global population.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature (Laursen et al., 2014; Chong et al., 2016; Insel, 2010) as indicated in the manuscript.

claim: Schizophrenia is associated with increased disability, mortality, and high private and social economic burden.
source: It is associated with increased disability, mortality, and high private and social economic burden (Laursen et al., 2014; Chong et al., 2016; Insel, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Biological changes underlying schizophrenia begin years prior to psychotic symptoms.
source: Although psychosis typically onsets during adolescence and young adulthood, there is accumulating data that demonstrates underlying biological changes, beginning years prior to the psychotic symptoms (Kahn and Sommer, 2015; Lewandowski et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Over 100 genetic variants have been identified contributing to the risk of schizophrenia.
source: Although over 100 genetic variants were identified contributing to the risk of schizophrenia, their broad distribution in the general population precludes clinical use (Stefansson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The broad distribution of schizophrenia genetic variants in the general population precludes their clinical use.
source: Although over 100 genetic variants were identified contributing to the risk of schizophrenia, their broad distribution in the general population precludes clinical use (Stefansson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents an inference from the genetic data.

claim: Brain imaging has demonstrated notable structural changes mostly in late and more chronic stages of schizophrenia.
source: Brain imaging has demonstrated notable structural changes mostly in late and more chronic stages of the disease, too late for useful intervention (McCutcheon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Circulating cell-free DNA in blood plasma was first discovered by Mandel and Metais in 1948.
source: Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in the blood plasma was first discovered by Mandel and Metais in 1948 (Liu, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical literature.

claim: cfDNA fragments are typically approximately 150 bp of double-stranded DNA.
source: Over the years it was established that these typically ~150 bp fragments of double-stranded DNA are released into the bloodstream during the process of cell death (Lo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: cfDNA fragments are released into the bloodstream during the process of cell death.
source: Over the years it was established that these typically ~150 bp fragments of double-stranded DNA are released into the bloodstream during the process of cell death (Lo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: cfDNA molecules have a half-life of approximately 15 minutes in circulation.
source: cfDNA molecules are rapidly cleared from the circulation with a half-life of ~15 min, thus reflecting events taking place at the time of blood draw (Lo et al., 1999; Sherwood and Weimer, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: cfDNA reflects events taking place at the time of blood draw.
source: cfDNA molecules are rapidly cleared from the circulation with a half-life of ~15 min, thus reflecting events taking place at the time of blood draw (Lo et al., 1999; Sherwood and Weimer, 2018).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the short half-life of cfDNA, supported by citations.

claim: Tissue-specific methylation patterns allow the identification of the tissue origins of cfDNA.
source: We and others have recently described an approach to identify the tissue origins of cfDNA, based on tissue-specific methylation patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research by the authors and others.

claim: Imaging studies demonstrate gray matter reduction in the frontal and temporo-limbic regions in schizophrenia.
source: The studies generally demonstrate gray matter reduction in the frontal and temporo-limbic regions (Takahashi and Suzuki, 2018; Dietsche et al., 2017; Pantelis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: Structural brain abnormalities in psychosis occur prior to full blown symptoms.
source: Structural brain abnormalities in psychosis occur prior to full blown symptoms and progressively worsen as psychosis develops.
evidence: This claim is supported by the preceding discussion of imaging studies and citations.

claim: Apoptosis has been proposed as a potential mechanism contributing to progressive brain pathology in schizophrenia.
source: Although the underlying causes and the exact timing of the morphologic changes in the brain remain obscure, apoptosis has been proposed as a potential mechanism that could contribute to this progressive pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: Post-mortem evidence shows regional reduction of neuronal and glia density in schizophrenia.
source: This idea is also supported by post-mortem evidence of regional reduction of neuronal and glia density.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to post-mortem studies (Jarskog et al., 2005; Jarskog, 2006).

claim: Apoptosis in the CNS occurs rapidly, and apoptotic cells are typically cleared within 24 hours.
source: Apoptosis in the CNS occurs rapidly, and apoptotic cells are typically cleared within 24 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Apoptosis in the CNS occurs without inflammation and does not involve gliosis.
source: The process occurs without inflammation and does not involve gliosis (Jarskog et al., 2005; Jarskog, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Ershove et al. demonstrated dysregulation of apoptosis in schizophrenia through considerably increased oxidated levels of cfDNA.
source: Ershove et al. demonstrated dysregulation of apoptosis in schizophrenia through considerably increased oxidated levels of cfDNA (Ershova et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: 13 genomic loci were selected that are unmethylated specifically in neurons (four markers), oligodendrocytes (three markers), or astrocytes (three markers) and in all brain-derived cell types (three markers), and methylated in all other examined cell types.
source: Using this comparative analysis we selected 13 genomic loci, which are unmethylated specifically in neurons (four markers), oligodendrocytes (three markers), or astrocytes (three markers) and in all brain-derived cell types (three markers), and methylated in all other examined cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis described in the methods and validated experimentally.

claim: The brain markers allowed the detection of as little as 0.1% brain DNA in a mixture, or just one brain genome in a mixture of a thousand genomes.
source: To determine assay sensitivity, we serially diluted brain DNA into leukocyte DNA, and found that the brain markers allowed the detection of as little as 0.1% brain DNA in a mixture, or just one brain genome in a mixture of a thousand genomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Total levels of cfDNA circulating in plasma were higher in patients with first psychotic episode compared with healthy controls (p-value = 0.017).
source: Total levels of cfDNA circulating in plasma were higher in patients with first psychotic episode compared with healthy controls (Mann-Whitney test for controls vs. patients, p-value = 0.017, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: cfDNA levels from all brain cells combined were higher in patients with first psychotic episode compared with healthy controls.
source: cfDNA levels from all brain cell combined were higher in patients with first psychotic episode compared with healthy (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Neuron-derived cfDNA levels were significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0013).
source: cfDNA levels from each brain cell type separately or from whole brain markers were also significantly elevated in patients (Mann-Whitney test for patients vs. controls, neurons p-value = 0.0013, astrocytes p-value = 0.0016, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0129, whole brain markers p-value = 0.0012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Astrocyte-derived cfDNA levels were significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0016).
source: cfDNA levels from each brain cell type separately or from whole brain markers were also significantly elevated in patients (Mann-Whitney test for patients vs. controls, neurons p-value = 0.0013, astrocytes p-value = 0.0016, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0129, whole brain markers p-value = 0.0012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Oligodendrocyte-derived cfDNA levels were significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0129).
source: cfDNA levels from each brain cell type separately or from whole brain markers were also significantly elevated in patients (Mann-Whitney test for patients vs. controls, neurons p-value = 0.0013, astrocytes p-value = 0.0016, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0129, whole brain markers p-value = 0.0012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Whole brain-derived cfDNA levels were significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0012).
source: cfDNA levels from each brain cell type separately or from whole brain markers were also significantly elevated in patients (Mann-Whitney test for patients vs. controls, neurons p-value = 0.0013, astrocytes p-value = 0.0016, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0129, whole brain markers p-value = 0.0012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Elevated brain-derived cfDNA was seen when measuring either its absolute concentration or its fraction.
source: Elevated brain-derived cfDNA was seen when measuring either its absolute concentration (Figure 1D) or its fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Elevated brain-derived cfDNA is consistent with elevated release of brain-derived cfDNA in patients with first psychotic episode, reflecting brain pathology, rather than a non-specific effect.
source: This is consistent with elevated release of brain-derived cfDNA in patients with first psychotic episode, reflecting brain pathology, rather than a non-specific effect.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that both absolute and fractional levels are elevated.

claim: The brain cfDNA score was able to identify the plasma of patients with a first psychotic episode with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.77 (p-value = 0.0003).
source: The brain cfDNA score was able to identify the plasma of patients with a first psychotic episode with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.77 (p-value = 0.0003).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At 90% specificity, the sensitivity for identifying patients with first psychotic episode was 65%.
source: At 90% specificity, the sensitivity for identifying patients with first psychotic episode was 65% (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was no significant correlation between brain markers and clinical parameters including the duration of the current episode, duration of hospitalization, or the number of psychotic episodes.
source: There was no significant correlation between brain markers and clinical parameters including the duration of the current episode, duration of hospitalization, or the number of psychotic episodes (see Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of clinical data.

claim: After correcting for multiple testing, no statistically significant correlation was found between drug intake and cfDNA.
source: After correcting for multiple testing, we did not find any statistically significant correlation between drug intake and cfDNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of medication data.

claim: Increased levels of brain-derived cfDNA were detected in adult patients with a first psychotic episode.
source: We have demonstrated increased levels of brain-derived cfDNA in adult patients with a first psychotic episode.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The study detected elevated brain cfDNA but did not reveal the cause of release of these molecules to circulation.
source: We note that our study detected elevated brain cfDNA but did not reveal the cause of release of these molecules to circulation.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of the study's limitations.

claim: Elevated brain cfDNA could result from brain cell apoptosis.
source: We hypothesize that our findings reflect brain cell apoptosis, which is consistent with the literature indicating brain damage in such patients.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on literature.

claim: Elevated brain cfDNA could result from a disruption of the blood-brain barrier.
source: However, elevated brain cfDNA could also result from a disruption of the blood-brain barrier, from a defect in the local removal of debris from dying brain cells, or a combination of these biological phenomena.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Elevated brain cfDNA could result from a defect in the local removal of debris from dying brain cells.
source: However, elevated brain cfDNA could also result from a disruption of the blood-brain barrier, from a defect in the local removal of debris from dying brain cells, or a combination of these biological phenomena.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Samples were obtained after the initial stabilization and partial remission of the psychotic symptoms.
source: We also note that samples were obtained after the initial stabilization and partial remission of the psychotic symptoms, suggesting the possibility that a more dramatic elevation of brain cfDNA takes place during the acute phase of the psychotic episode.
evidence: This is a description of the study design and timing of sample collection.

claim: A more dramatic elevation of brain cfDNA may take place during the acute phase of the psychotic episode.
source: We also note that samples were obtained after the initial stabilization and partial remission of the psychotic symptoms, suggesting the possibility that a more dramatic elevation of brain cfDNA takes place during the acute phase of the psychotic episode.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the timing of sample collection.

claim: An elevation in the total concentration of cfDNA was observed among psychotic patients.
source: Finally, we observed an elevation in the total concentration of cfDNA among psychotic patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Brain cfDNA comprises less than 1% of total cfDNA even among patients.
source: Since brain cfDNA comprises a small fraction of cfDNA even among patients (<1% of total cfDNA), this elevation must originate in other tissues.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data showing the fraction of brain-derived cfDNA.

claim: The elevation in total cfDNA must originate in tissues other than brain.
source: Since brain cfDNA comprises a small fraction of cfDNA even among patients (<1% of total cfDNA), this elevation must originate in other tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small fraction of brain-derived cfDNA.

claim: Elevated total cfDNA can be related to drug toxicity, stress mechanisms, or derive from immune or inflammatory cells.
source: Elevated total cfDNA can be related to drug toxicity, stress mechanisms, or more likely derive from immune or inflammatory cells, perhaps related to the proposed link between schizophrenia and the immune system (Zengeler and Lukens, 2021; Khandaker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to literature on schizophrenia and the immune system.

claim: The study recruited 29 patients with first psychotic episode and 31 healthy controls.
source: We determined the plasma concentrations of brain-derived cfDNA (including methylation markers of neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes and whole brain) in 31 healthy controls, and 29 patients with first psychotic episode.
evidence: This is a description of the study design and sample size.

claim: The study included 55% females (n=16) and 45% males (n=13), with an age distribution of 18–48 years (average 24).
source: The study included 55% females (n=16) and 45% males (n=13), with an age distribution of 18–48 years (average 24).
evidence: This is a description of the demographic characteristics of the study population.

claim: 72.5% of the patients (n=21) were hospitalized with a first psychotic event in their life.
source: 72.5% of the patients (n=21) were hospitalized with a first psychotic event in their life, and 27.5% of the patients (n=8) had a second or third psychotic event, up to a year after the beginning of the first one, which clinically can be considered as the first psychotic event in life that has not reached complete and stable remission.
evidence: This is a description of the clinical characteristics of the study population.

claim: 44.8% of the patients (n=13) did not have any background of drug abuse.
source: 44.8% of the patients (n=13) did not have any background of drug abuse, 31% (n=9) indicated the use of marijuana in the weeks preceding the onset of the first psychotic episode.
evidence: This is a description of the substance use history of the study population.

claim: 31% of patients (n=9) indicated the use of marijuana in the weeks preceding the onset of the first psychotic episode.
source: 44.8% of the patients (n=13) did not have any background of drug abuse, 31% (n=9) indicated the use of marijuana in the weeks preceding the onset of the first psychotic episode.
evidence: This is a description of the substance use history of the study population.

claim: Treatment with bisulfite led to degradation of 60–90% of the DNA (average, 75% degradation).
source: Treatment with bisulfite led to degradation of 60–90% of the DNA (average, 75% degradation), consistent with previous reports (Grunau et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation and citation to previous reports.

claim: DNA degradation from bisulfite treatment does not significantly harm assay specificity since methylated and unmethylated molecules are equally affected.
source: Note that while DNA degradation does reduce assay sensitivity (since fewer DNA molecules are available for PCR amplification), it does not significantly harm assay specificity since methylated and unmethylated molecules are equally affected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of bisulfite treatment.

claim: The majority of patients stabilized within 4 weeks (79%).
source: The time achieving stability was different for each individual patient, but the majority stabilized within 4 weeks (79%).
evidence: This is a description of the clinical course of the study population.

claim: Neuron-derived cfDNA percentage was significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0048).
source: Mann-Whitney test for controls vs. patients, neurons p-value = 0.0048, astrocytes p-value = 0.0074, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0186, and whole brain markers p-value = 0.0018.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Astrocyte-derived cfDNA percentage was significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0074).
source: Mann-Whitney test for controls vs. patients, neurons p-value = 0.0048, astrocytes p-value = 0.0074, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0186, and whole brain markers p-value = 0.0018.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Oligodendrocyte-derived cfDNA percentage was significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0186).
source: Mann-Whitney test for controls vs. patients, neurons p-value = 0.0048, astrocytes p-value = 0.0074, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0186, and whole brain markers p-value = 0.0018.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Whole brain-derived cfDNA percentage was significantly elevated in patients with first psychotic episode compared to controls (p-value = 0.0018).
source: Mann-Whitney test for controls vs. patients, neurons p-value = 0.0048, astrocytes p-value = 0.0074, oligodendrocytes p-value = 0.0186, and whole brain markers p-value = 0.0018.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The markers of each brain cell type were able to identify the plasma of patients with first psychotic episode with an AUC of 0.65–0.73.
source: The markers of each brain cell type were able to identify the plasma of patients with first psychotic episode with an AUC of 0.65–0.73 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: Nominally statistically significant correlations were found between the levels of brain-derived cfDNA and drug intake for one type of astrocyte marker (PRDM2) and one type of neuron marker (ITF).
source: We found nominally statistically significant correlations between the levels of brain-derived cfDNA and drug intake for only one type of astrocyte marker (PRDM2) and one type of neuron marker (ITF) (Spearman correlation coefficient for astrocyte marker PRDM2: p-value = 0.024/drugs on blood test day, and p-value = 0.025/overall amount drugs; for neuron ITF: p-value = 0.016/overall amount of drugs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of medication data.

claim: Brain-specific cfDNA methylation markers can potentially assist early detection and monitoring of schizophrenia and thus allow early intervention and adequate therapy.
source: Brain-specific cfDNA methylation markers can potentially assist early detection and monitoring of schizophrenia and thus allow early intervention and adequate therapy.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential clinical applications based on the study findings.

claim: The etiology of schizophrenia is multifactorial, with a complex interaction of polygenic risk and environmental factors.
source: The etiology of schizophrenia is multifactorial, with a complex interaction of polygenic risk and environmental factors (Insel, 2010; Owen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Plasma levels of cfDNA vary over time depending on age, increased physical activity, and the existence of various medical conditions such as infectious diseases.
source: It is known that plasma levels of cfDNA vary over time depending on age, increased physical activity, and the existence of various medical conditions such as infectious diseases (Sherwood and Weimer, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Cell-type-specific methylation markers allow the inference of cell death in multiple settings, for example, cardiomyocyte cell death following myocardial infarction or hepatocyte death in patients with liver metastasis.
source: Such cell-type-specific markers allow the inference of cell death in multiple settings, for example, cardiomyocyte cell death following myocardial infarction or hepatocyte death in patients with liver metastasis (Lehmann-Werman et al., 2018; Lehmann-Werman et al., 2016; Zemmour et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2015; Gai et al., 2018; Lubotzky et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Data describing the development and validation of 10 cell-specific markers (neurons, oligodendrocytes, and astrocytes) were published in a recent paper.
source: Data describing the development and validation of these 10 cell-specific markers (neurons, oligodendrocytes, and astrocytes) were published in a recent paper (Lubotzky et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claim: Elevated brain cfDNA provides an intriguing, measurable link between a physical process in the brain and a psychotic episode.
source: Regardless, elevated brain cfDNA provides an intriguing, measurable link between a physical process in the brain and a psychotic episode.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study findings.

claim: Elevated cfDNA can reflect ongoing changes in the brain of patients with schizophrenia in early stages that are too subtle to be seen by imaging techniques.
source: Elevated cfDNA can reflect ongoing changes in the brain of patients with schizophrenia in early stages that are too subtle to be seen by imaging techniques.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential utility of the biomarker.

claim: The short half-life of cfDNA in the plasma and time of blood sampling (a few weeks after admission in most cases) suggest that pathological brain processes occur for a longer period than the acute presentation.
source: On the other hand, taking into account the short half-life of cfDNA in the plasma and time of blood sampling (a few weeks after admission in most cases), our results suggest that pathological brain processes occur for a longer period than the acute presentation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of sample collection and the known half-life of cfDNA.

claim: Brain changes emerge around onset of schizophrenia and accumulate over the years of the disease.
source: This is also supported by the literature as brain changes emerging around onset of the schizophrenia and accumulate over the years of the disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the literature discussed earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Increased brain-derived cfDNA can be a marker of psychotic exacerbation in chronic schizophrenia.
source: Increased brain-derived cfDNA can be a marker of psychotic exacerbation in chronic schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.
